I’d make **301: Deploy Your Gesture Dial with ExecuTorch**—a two-hour workshop that extends 201 using the same UNO Q, Knob, Pixels, and Vibro hardware.

The series progression becomes:

| Series | Focus |
|---|---|
| 10x | Connect hardware and build interactions |
| 20x | Collect data, train models, and evaluate predictions |
| **30x** | **Export, deploy, and measure PyTorch models on-device** |

**What attendees build**

A dial that recognizes `flick_left`, `flick_right`, and `wiggle` using a small PyTorch neural network deployed through ExecuTorch. Predictions trigger the existing LED and haptic feedback.

Use **ExecuTorch with XNNPACK on the UNO Q’s Linux MPU**, with the MCU handling sensors and outputs through Bridge. XNNPACK supports ARM64 Linux; this is a plausible deployment path that still needs validation inside App Lab. [ExecuTorch XNNPACK documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/backends/xnnpack/xnnpack-overview.html)

Keep Qualcomm accelerator integration outside the core session until support for this exact board and OS is demonstrated. ExecuTorch’s backend matrix currently lists its Qualcomm backend under Android. [Backend matrix](https://github.com/pytorch/executorch/blob/main/docs/source/backends-overview.md)

**Model and architecture**

Reuse 201’s capture flow and 16-value feature representation. Start with a tiny network: `16 → 32 → 3`, with ReLU between layers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Laptop: train PyTorch model"] --> B["Export and lower to XNNPACK"]
    B --> C["gesture.pte"]
    C --> D["UNO Q Linux: ExecuTorch"]
    E["Knob → MCU"] -->|Bridge| F["Linux: capture and extract features"]
    F --> D
    D -->|Bridge| G["MCU → Pixels + Vibro"]
```

Train and export on attendees’ laptops; run inference locally on the board. Embed feature normalization in the exported model and ship explicit label ordering alongside it.

Use a supplied dataset recorded across several people, plus fresh attendee recordings for evaluation. The fifteen examples used in 201 are useful for its centroid exercise, but should not be assumed sufficient for a neural network.

**Two-hour agenda**

| Time | Activity | Checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| 0–15 min | Run a supplied `.pte` and inspect the architecture | Dial produces predictions |
| 15–35 min | Inspect data, train the small network | Evaluate on held-out recordings |
| 35–55 min | Export, lower, and compare outputs | PyTorch and ExecuTorch agree within tolerance |
| 55–75 min | Deploy the model through App Lab | Personal export controls physical feedback |
| 75–100 min | Test unfamiliar users and ambiguous gestures | Record errors and rejection behavior |
| 100–120 min | Measure and compare with 201 | Explain accuracy, latency, and deployment tradeoffs |

Split data by recording session or participant to avoid testing on near-duplicates of training examples. Treat softmax values as model scores, not calibrated certainty; explicitly test confident mistakes.

**Preparation and implementation scope**

Create a self-contained `301-executorch-dial/` workshop containing:

- A README with prerequisites, deployment instructions, and troubleshooting.
- Laptop training/export scripts, a small dataset, and fixed evaluation fixtures.
- An App Lab project adapted from 201, with ExecuTorch inference and packaged model assets.
- A matching `workshop-app.zip`.
- One regression check covering preprocessing, label mapping, export parity, and invalid inputs.

Before publishing, validate a pinned PyTorch/ExecuTorch combination in the actual App Lab environment. Preinstall dependencies and provide a known-good model so export problems do not prevent attendees completing the hardware exercise.

Measure model loading time, warm inference latency, artifact size, and gesture-to-feedback latency separately. The existing capture window and end-of-motion delay may dominate perceived responsiveness; a tiny model does not guarantee a noticeable speedup.

**Completion criterion:** attendees can export a model, run it offline on UNO Q, demonstrate physical feedback, and explain one measured tradeoff against 201’s classifier.

No repository files changed or hardware checks run. The main unresolved risk is ExecuTorch runtime compatibility inside the selected UNO Q App Lab image.

I’d make **301: Knock Code — Teach a Box Its Secret Rhythm**.

Attendees tap the Modulino Knob’s button in a short rhythm. A small neural network running through **ExecuTorch on the UNO Q** recognizes the rhythm and responds with a distinctive light-and-haptic sequence. Think “knock-knock … knock” as a physical command.

This gives the workshop its own identity: **a rhythm-controlled interface**, using the same Knob, Pixels, and Vibro.

**The interaction**

1. Turn the knob to select one of three commands to teach.
2. Press the button to perform a rhythm; Pixels show recording progress.
3. Record several examples at different speeds.
4. Train and export the model on a laptop.
5. Deploy it to the UNO Q and perform a rhythm to trigger its command.

Example commands:

| Rhythm | Response |
|---|---|
| Two quick taps, pause, one tap | A green welcome animation |
| Three evenly spaced taps | A traveling blue light |
| One tap, pause, two quick taps | A purple celebration with haptic pulses |

Provide a pretrained model and sample recordings so everyone can start with a working experience before teaching their own patterns. Haptic playback happens after recording ends to avoid disrupting the input.

**Where ExecuTorch fits**

The MCU timestamps button presses and releases, debounces them, and drives the outputs. Linux receives completed tap sequences through Bridge and converts them into a fixed-size input containing press durations, gaps, and a validity mask.

A small PyTorch network learns the timing patterns. Attendees export it to `.pte`, then run it with **ExecuTorch’s XNNPACK CPU backend on the UNO Q’s Linux side**.

Normalize timing to help recognize the same rhythm performed faster or slower, while retaining total duration as an additional feature. Include miscellaneous rhythms in the dataset and evaluate rejection of unfamiliar patterns. This is a playful command interface; recognition is not authentication.

**Two-hour workshop**

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–15 min | Try the working rhythm box and trace input → inference → feedback |
| 15–35 min | Record labeled rhythms and inspect their timing |
| 35–55 min | Train a tiny network using supplied data plus personal examples |
| 55–75 min | Export to ExecuTorch and check output agreement |
| 75–95 min | Deploy to UNO Q and connect predictions to feedback |
| 95–120 min | Challenge it with different tempos, unfamiliar rhythms, and another person |

The central lesson is **taking a custom PyTorch model from recorded physical input to a deployed interactive device**.

For implementation, I’d use `301-knock-code/`, with a self-contained App Lab project, laptop training/export script, sample dataset, pretrained `.pte`, and a small export-parity regression check. The first prototype should verify reliable MCU button timestamps and ExecuTorch execution inside App Lab before building the full lesson.

Planning only; no files changed or board tests run. Runtime compatibility and recognition quality remain to be verified on the UNO Q.

**301: Color Detective** — point a USB camera at an object, and the UNO Q identifies its color using a small vision model running in ExecuTorch.

The Modulinos make it a physical guessing game:

- **Knob:** choose a target color, such as red.
- **Pixels:** display the target color.
- **Knob button:** take a snapshot and run inference.
- **Vibro:** pulse when the detected color matches the target.

Attendees hunt for matching objects around the room. Everything runs locally on the UNO Q.

The workshop uses a supplied pretrained model, so participants focus on **exporting to ExecuTorch, deploying, and connecting predictions to hardware**. No data collection or training required. A 60–90 minute session ends with experiments under different lighting and backgrounds.

Color detection can also use simple image-processing rules; that makes a useful comparison when discussing whether a model is necessary.

A USB camera captures one of three simple faces: **happy, sad, or surprised**. A supplied model runs through **ExecuTorch on the UNO Q’s Linux side**.

- **Press the Knob** to capture and classify.

The activity is straightforward: **show a card → press → get a reaction**. Attendees can then draw their own faces and see what confuses the model.

For a **60–90 minute workshop**, participants run the supplied demo, export the pretrained PyTorch model to ExecuTorch, deploy it, and customize the physical responses. No attendee training step.

**301: Beat the Board** — a game where the UNO Q tries to predict your next move.

Uses just **Knob, Pixels, and Vibro**:

1. Turn the knob to choose **left or right**, then press to commit.
2. Pixels reveal whether the board predicted your choice.
3. A vibration means it caught you. Fool it to earn a point.

**The AI:** a tiny sequence model running in **ExecuTorch** predicts your next choice from your previous choices. It locks in its prediction **before you make your move**. Try alternating, repeating, or inventing patterns—and see when it catches on.

Use a supplied pretrained model that recognizes common choice patterns. It uses recent play as input; no training step is needed during the game. Random choices should remain unpredictable.

**A 60–90 minute workshop:** play the game, inspect the model’s inputs, export the supplied PyTorch model to `.pte`, deploy it on UNO Q, and compare its success rate against a simple “repeat your last choice” baseline.

The identity is **a physical game against a predictive opponent**, with ExecuTorch powering the opponent.

Skipped extra hardware and attendee model training. The model’s predictive usefulness and ExecuTorch runtime still need validation on UNO Q.

*** Add File: /Users/aaishika/Developer/Qualcomm/uno-q-workshops/301-beat-the-board/README.md
+# QC UNO Q Workshop 301: Beat the Board
+
+> Planning draft. The app, model, and import ZIP are not implemented yet. ExecuTorch integration and physical behavior require validation on the UNO Q before this workshop is ready to run.
+
+Can you be unpredictable? Build a tabletop game where an AI opponent guesses whether you will choose left or right. Fool it to win a point; get caught and the board scores instead.
+
+This standalone 90-minute workshop introduces deploying a PyTorch model with ExecuTorch. It uses only the UNO Q, Modulino Knob, Pixels, and Vibro. No camera, microphone, cloud service, or attendee model training is required.
+
+## Learning outcomes
+
+Attendees will:
+
+- Turn a short history of choices into a model input.
+- Export a supplied PyTorch model to an ExecuTorch `.pte` artifact.
+- Run inference on the UNO Q Linux MPU and connect results to MCU-controlled hardware.
+- Compare a learned predictor with simple baselines and recognize the limits of predicting random choices.
+
+Basic Python and familiarity with starting an App Lab project are recommended. No earlier workshop is required.
+
+## Hardware and preparation
+
+- Arduino UNO Q, USB-C cable, and attendee laptop.
+- Modulino Knob, Pixels, and Vibro, connected using three Qwiic cables.
+- Arduino App Lab installed and the board provisioned before the session.
+- A tested, pinned laptop export environment and board runtime, supplied by the instructor.
+
+Wiring: `UNO Q Qwiic → Knob → Pixels → Vibro`.
+
+The instructor supplies a working App Lab ZIP, pretrained weights, exported model, export script, and evaluation examples. All required packages and artifacts must be downloaded before the session; gameplay and export should work offline afterward. Exact package versions and installation commands will be documented after the compatibility prototype passes.
+
+## The game
+
+### One match
+
+1. Make eight unscored left/right choices to establish a history. Pixels fill one at a time to show warm-up progress.
+2. Play sixteen scored rounds. Every round awards one point: the board scores if it predicts correctly; otherwise the player scores.
+3. The higher score wins. An 8–8 result is a draw.
+4. Press and release the knob on the result screen to start a new match, clearing scores and history.
+
+### One round
+
+1. With choice input disabled, Linux predicts from the last eight committed choices and stores the prediction with the round number.
+2. The MCU opens selection only after that prediction is locked. A neutral light indicates that the board is ready; its prediction stays hidden.
+3. Turn left to select left or right to select right. The latest turn direction selects the side; rotation distance does not matter. The corresponding half of the Pixels lights up. Each round starts with no selection, so an accidental press alone cannot submit a move.
+4. Press the knob to commit. The MCU captures the selected side once. Linux compares it against the locked prediction, updates the score, then appends the choice to history.
+5. Reveal the predicted side briefly. If the board caught the player, all Pixels flash twice and Vibro gives one short pulse. If the player fooled it, an outward light sweep celebrates the point.
+6. Show the score briefly, then wait for the button to be released before preparing the next round.
+
+No time limit is needed. Inputs during reveal and scoring are ignored. Debounce the button on the MCU, retain a committed event until acknowledged, and identify it by round number so repeated Bridge reads cannot award duplicate points. Reset discards any pending event. Keep animations nonblocking.
+
+Use the left four Pixels for player score and the right four for board score, with each Pixel representing four points and partial brightness indicating progress within that group. The App Lab console gives exact scores, round numbers, predictions, and outcomes. Position and animation distinguish states as well as color. Tune brightness and vibration on the actual hardware.
+
+## The AI opponent
+
+Use a small feed-forward network: `8 inputs → Linear(8, 32) → ReLU → Linear(32, 2)`. This is a 354-parameter model with a fixed input shape and simple operators.
+
+| Contract | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| Input | Float32 tensor of shape `[1, 8]` |
+| Encoding | Left = -1, right = +1, oldest choice first |
+| Output | Two logits, `[left, right]` |
+| Prediction | Largest logit; exact ties choose left |
+| State | Last eight committed choices, stored by the game |
+| Updates | History changes after each round; model weights stay fixed |
+
+The first eight moves avoid padding and special cold-start behavior. Run one inference per scored round. The model receives no live knob position, pending selection, timing, or button state. Its scores are not presented as calibrated confidence.
+
+### Instructor training
+
+Train offline using reproducible synthetic choice sequences: repeated sides, alternating sides, short repeating blocks, biased random choices, and patterns with occasional mistakes or switches. Include balanced independent random sequences to demonstrate the limit of prediction. Use next-choice cross-entropy training and ship the resulting weights; attendees need not train during the core session.
+
+Split complete sequences before extracting overlapping windows. Keep evaluation seeds separate and reserve some pattern types for generalization tests. Synthetic patterns can establish a working demonstration but do not establish predictive skill against people. Pilot the game with several players before making claims about recognizing human habits.
+
+Compare the model against “repeat the previous choice,” “choose the opposite,” and a seeded random baseline on identical histories. Report results separately for each sequence family. Balanced random play should produce approximately 50% accuracy over a large evaluation set; one sixteen-round match is too short to establish statistical performance.
+
+The model need not beat every heuristic. The teaching question is when a learned predictor helps, when a simpler rule works, and when the available input contains no useful signal.
+
+## Deployment architecture
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+    W[Supplied PyTorch weights] --> E[Laptop: export and lower to XNNPACK]
+    E --> P[opponent.pte]
+    P --> R[UNO Q Linux: ExecuTorch runtime]
+    H[Committed choice history] --> R
+    R --> L[Lock prediction before opening selection]
+    L --> G[Linux: game and scoring]
+    K[Knob] --> M[MCU: input and feedback]
+    M -->|Bridge: committed choice| G
+    G --> H
+    G -->|Bridge: round state and outcome| M
+    M --> O[Pixels and Vibro]
+```
+
+Target ExecuTorch's XNNPACK CPU backend on the Linux MPU. Its documentation lists ARM64 Linux support and the PyTorch export/lowering path. This establishes a candidate deployment route, not verified App Lab compatibility. See the [XNNPACK documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/backends/xnnpack/xnnpack-overview.html) and [UNO Q hardware documentation](https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/uno-q/).
+
+Prefer the Python runtime binding in the App Lab Python process. Load the model once at startup, check its input/output contract, and keep the same runtime instance for the match. Pin a mutually tested exporter/runtime combination and include model metadata describing encoding, label order, version, and artifact hash. Verify export delegation rather than assuming the chosen operators use XNNPACK.
+
+If the binding cannot run inside the selected App Lab image, resolve packaging before writing the attendee instructions. A custom C++ integration is outside the initial scope. A missing, incompatible, or invalid model stops gameplay with a clear console error and visible error pattern; do not silently substitute a heuristic for ExecuTorch.
+
+## Session plan: 90 minutes
+
+| Time | Activity | Observable result |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| 0–10 min | Wire the modules and run the supplied app | Complete a match |
+| 10–20 min | Try repetition, alternation, and deliberate unpredictability | Explain what the board can observe |
+| 20–35 min | Inspect history encoding and the tiny PyTorch model | Predict the input for an example round |
+| 35–50 min | Export supplied weights, lower to XNNPACK, compare outputs | Create a `.pte` that passes parity checks |
+| 50–65 min | Deploy the export and restart the App Lab project | Play against the attendee's exported artifact |
+| 65–80 min | Compare model and baseline results on fixed histories | Identify one success and one failure |
+| 80–90 min | Swap players, discuss limits, recap the deployment path | Explain why random play remains difficult |
+
+The supplied `.pte` is a recovery path for laptop setup problems. Attendees who use it can complete the hardware exercise, but their export checkpoint remains incomplete. Offer a 60-minute version by demonstrating export centrally and shortening the experiments.
+
+## Implementation sequence and deliverables
+
+All proposed files below belong to this workshop and are not present yet.
+
+1. **Prove runtime compatibility.** Export the tiny model and run a known input in the actual App Lab environment on a UNO Q. Record board image, architecture, Python version, package versions, memory use, and successful model load. This is the first go/no-go gate.
+2. **Prepare the opponent.** Add `training/train.py`, `training/export.py`, pinned dependencies, supplied weights, and deterministic evaluation fixtures. Verify numerical parity and measure pattern-specific accuracy before designing the lesson around the results.
+3. **Build the game.** Add `workshop-app/python/main.py`, a small `game.py` for round state/scoring, model assets and metadata, `sketch/sketch.ino`, `sketch/sketch.yaml`, and `app.yaml`. Keep the MCU hardware services and Linux state machine local to this workshop.
+4. **Verify and package.** Add `test_beat_the_board.py` for game logic and a focused export/runtime check. Produce `workshop-app.zip` preserving the repository's App Lab archive layout, then test a clean import.
+5. **Pilot and publish.** Run the lesson with first-time participants, tune physical feedback, replace this draft with tested setup instructions, and add 301 to the root catalog under a proposed “30x: Model deployment with ExecuTorch” section.
+
+No dashboard, account system, persistent player profile, online training, accelerator integration, or quantization is needed for the first version. Scores and history stay in memory and reset on restart.
+
+## Verification and release gates
+
+- **Fairness:** prove inference precedes input enablement; changing the pending choice cannot change the locked prediction. Log the locked round number before selection opens, but reveal the prediction only after commit.
+- **Game correctness:** eight warm-up moves do not score; sixteen scored rounds award exactly sixteen total points; duplicate/stale events cannot score; restart clears history; button hold/release cannot submit an extra round.
+- **Model contract:** reject malformed shape, invalid choice encoding, missing artifacts, and non-finite outputs. Export parity checks compare logits within a documented float32 tolerance and verify identical selected labels on fixed fixtures.
+- **Predictive usefulness:** show useful results on held-out structured sequences, report each baseline, and check roughly chance performance on many balanced random sequences. If the structured-pattern demonstration is unreliable, improve the training data before publishing.
+- **Physical behavior:** verify orientation, debounce, selection changes, no-selection presses, sustained presses, feedback timing, Bridge interruption, and reset/restart on actual modules. A communication error pauses the round rather than inventing a move.
+- **Deployment:** import the ZIP into a clean App Lab project, compile the sketch, load the artifact, and play a full match with networking disabled after provisioning. Verify the packaged source and model match the tested files.
+- **Performance:** separately record model load time, warm inference latency, and button-to-feedback latency. Aim for feedback within 150 ms of commit, excluding the deliberate reveal animation; this is a design target, not a measured result.
+
+Success means an attendee can play a complete match, run an exported model through ExecuTorch on the UNO Q, and explain both the prediction-before-choice rule and one limitation of the opponent.
*** End Patch"));

+
+Can you be unpredictable? Play a tabletop game against an AI opponent that guesses whether you will choose left or right. Fool it to win a point; get caught and the board scores instead.

+## Before the workshop

+2. Clone this repository and prepare the export environment below on your laptop.
+3. Import and run the supplied app once while online so App Lab can install its dependencies. Complete downloads before the session.
